title: The road ahead - what do RSEs need from TREs?
abstract:
Join us for an engaging workshop where we’ll be working together to set the development direction for Trusted Research Environments.We'll kick off with insights from our experience implementing TREs and some of the challenges and solutions we’ve faced along the way. As an interactive workshop we’ll then explore critical aspects of TREs, from security, to collaboration tools, and data management to user experience and set the direction for future TRE development.Through hands-on activities, attendees will:
Gain insights into TRE development and implementation
Directly contribute to the TRE community framework
Collaborate on solutions to pressing challenges in research environments
Connect with peers and experts in secure research platforms
Whether you're a seasoned TRE user or new to the concept, your expertise will help shape the tools driving the future of collaborative research. Join us to make your mark on the evolving landscape of Trusted Research Environments and gain actionable insights for your own projects.

title: Sustainable Funding for Scientific Software
abstract:
We know that it has historically been challenging to secure adequate funding for software development across the lifecycle, particularly for non-coding elements, and for foundational software that falls outside a specific scientific domain.
At Wellcome, we are increasingly seeing the impact of these funding issues across our programmes and partnerships – and therefore have been working to understand how we can more effectively support software. We have been exploring the funding gaps and needs of software developers, the role of funders in fostering enabling environments for ‘healthy’ software, and the design of sustainable financial models.
In this workshop, we’ll share some of our findings and the emergent thinking on how our future funding models should be shaped in response, with space for you to share your feedback and ideas. We will also highlight any current opportunities for funding.

title: R Development Hackathon
abstract: The R programming language is widely used in statistics and data analytics. It first appeared in 1993, and its first stable (1.0.0) release was in 2000. It has been maintained by a motivated team of volunteers since its creation. To continue its widespread success, however, we need to ensure that we can maintain the maintainers of the R project. Recently, there has been a movement to upskill more members of the community in how to make contributions to R, in the form of the “R Contribution Working Group” (https://contributor.r-project.org/). One initiative of this group is the organisation of “R Dev Days” where people come together to contribute to the code and documentation that gets distributed in binary versions of R (base R, the recommended packages and the Windows/macOS GUIs). This hackathon will follow the format of these Dev Days, where current and novice contributors work collaboratively on selected issues, with the goal of making progress on these issues and learning more about the R Development process along the way.

title: Large language models surpass human experts in predicting neuroscience results
abstract: Scientific discoveries often hinge on synthesizing decades of research, a task that potentially outstrips human information processing capacities. Large language models (LLMs) offer a solution. LLMs trained on the vast scientific literature could potentially integrate noisy yet interrelated findings to forecast novel results better than human experts. To evaluate this possibility, we created BrainBench, a forward-looking benchmark for predicting neuroscience results. We find that LLMs surpass experts in predicting experimental outcomes. BrainGPT, an LLM we tuned on the neuroscience literature, performed better yet. Like human experts, when LLMs were confident in their predictions, they were more likely to be correct, which presages a future where humans and LLMs team together to make discoveries. Our approach is not neuroscience-specific and is transferable to other knowledge-intensive endeavours. This work was supported by Microsoft, made possible through using ND A100 v4 series virtual machines on Microsoft Azure.

title: Introduction to the National AI Research Resource (AIRR) Using Dawn
abstract:
In 2023, the UK government funded the establishment of the AI Research Resource (AIRR), significantly increasing the availability of GPUs for machine learning and artificial intelligence researchers in the UK. AIRR comprises two new major systems: Dawn, located at the University of Cambridge, and Isambard-AI at the University of Bristol.
This workshop will provide an introduction to AIRR and offer hands-on experience with Dawn. Participants will engage in small-scale machine learning tasks using the same software stack required for large-scale ML training.
N.B.: To participate in the hands-on portion of the workshop, please register in advance to allow us to set up the necessary training accounts.

title: RSE Worldwide: Opportunities to Strengthen the Global RSE Community
abstract:
Research Software Engineering communities around the world continue to go from strength to strength. Recent years have seen the emergence of regional and national conferences and associations, with national and international RSE cooperation reaching new heights.
However, there are still many regions where RSEng is happening without structured support or established networks, and these RSEs could benefit from a connection with the global community. Specific regional and cultural context means that each community must find its own strengths and overcome its own challenges. Nevertheless, lessons learned and approaches taken in one community are likely to be valuable to others.
This session provides a platform for members of the diverse global community to meet, network, and share experiences and perspectives. Emerging communities can benefit from the experiences of more established networks, while longer-standing communities can better understand the international impact of RSEng. 
The growing number of events dedicated to RSEng taking place around the world is an encouraging sign of the strength and ongoing success of the RSE movement, but carries the threat of a “siloing” effect as local and regional groups focus ever more inward. This session presents an opportunity to discuss how we – as members of the international RSE community – can foster strong, vibrant local communities while reaping the benefits of international coordination and cooperation.

title: Cross-functional teams for challenge-led research
abstract:
As research becomes increasingly interdisciplinary and increasingly reliant on data and software to deliver impact, bringing together the range and diversity of talent required to effectively deliver impact from this research becomes increasingly important.
As the UK's national institute for data science and artificial intelligence, The Alan Turing Institute has recognised the importance of this from its inception, with research software engineering and project management teams in place from the beginning, and expanding its range of research infrastructure and delivery roles over the years to include research data scientists, research computing engineers, research community managers, research application managers and research data wranglers. These roles work across the Institute's research portfolio to help bridge the gap between research and practice and support effective collaboration across our wide range of partners in academia, industry and government.
As the Institute looks forward to its next 5 years, it is increasingly focussing its research around larger, impact-focussed, challenge-led missions. In this talk we will outline the vision for each of our challenge areas and how we are organising our research and innovation activity within each of these. We will also share our previous experiences of working on mission-shaped work at the Institute, and how bringing together teams of all the talents across a range of roles has been critical to successfully achieving our desired impact. Finally, we will talk about how we organise and operate the various research infrastructure and delivery teams at the Turing and how we see this evolving as we look to most effectively support the Institute's challenge-led missions.

title: Strategic Support for Computer Science Research at TU Delft: A Tailored Approach by the Research Engineering and Infrastructure Team
abstract:
In response to the evolving needs of research groups across computer science (CS) departments in TU Delft, the Research Engineering and Infrastructure Team (REIT) was established as a dedicated support pillar for CS research activities. 
Unlike other support teams at the university, REIT is uniquely dedicated to providing personalized, low-barrier research support that spans a broad spectrum of expertise—from high-performance computing (HPC) and infrastructure technology to specialized fields such as artificial intelligence (AI) and data-intensive applications.  
This presentation sheds light on REIT’s strategic engagements and activities aimed at enhancing infrastructure support and fulfilling various other research support roles. Our approach focuses on identifying and aligning with stakeholders: engaging with individual CS research groups to understand and meet their specific needs, partnership with ICT teams to align on infrastructure policies, and coordinating the technical implementation of solutions and procurement of resources. We also liaise with other research groups requiring similar compute infrastructure to ensure that our developments meet the specialized demands of AI research across the university; while maintaining ties with other TU Delft support teams to share lessons learned and best practices. 
Through these comprehensive efforts, REIT not only supports but actively accelerates innovation, catering to the nuanced needs of researchers of CS@TUDelft. We will reflect on the lessons learned since REIT's inception and highlight key projects that have significantly advanced the research landscape at our institution.

title: Collaborative Lesson Development Training for RSEs
abstract:
The Carpentries is a community building global capacity in essential data and computational skills for conducting efficient, open, and reproducible research. In addition to certified Instructors teaching Data Carpentry, Library Carpentry, and Software Carpentry workshops around the world, the community also includes many people contributing to and maintaining Open Source lessons.
Recent years have seen enormous growth in the number and diversity of lessons the community is creating, including many teaching skills and concepts essential to Research Software Engineering: software packaging and publication, environment and workflow management, containerised computing, etc. As this curriculum community has developed, demand has been growing for training opportunities, teaching how to design and develop Open Source curriculum effectively and in collaboration with others.
A new program launched in 2023, The Carpentries Collaborative Lesson Development Training teaches good practices in lesson design and development, and open source collaboration skills, using The Carpentries Workbench, an Open Source infrastructure for building accessible lesson websites.
As the discipline of Research Software Engineering continues to develop and mature, there is an increasing need for high-quality, Open Source and community-maintained training, and for the expertise to develop those resources. This poster will provide an overview of the training, explain how it meets this need, and describe how it fits into The Carpentries ecosystem for lesson development. It will also explain how RSEs can enroll in the training, and give examples of lesson projects that have benefited from it already.

title: Advanced Python Testing - mocking, property based testing, snapshot testing
abstract:
In this walkthrough, take your Python testing skills to the next level. Tired of waiting for network requests, writing millions of edge cases and copy pasting outputs for testing? This walkthrough is for you. We will cover mocking external libraries and HTTP calls, property based testing, and using a snapshot testing library to make writing tests easier, faster and more fun!

Mocking libraries allows us to test a code interface without requiring the underlying code to be run. This can be useful in testing databases and network requests without having to actually setup a database, or be connected to the Internet.

Property based testing checks that a particular property is satisfied by the code. Rather than list specific instances of a property, property based testing frameworks allow you to describe the property and (possibly) find counterexamples.

Snapshot based testing is useful for regression tests - to capture the output of a system at a particular state and ensure that it does not change. While snapshot based testing can be emulated using the standard Python library, it can be cumbersome to manually keep track of outputs. Snapshot testing libraries help with this.

title: Green RSEs? Building a community to reduce the environmental impacts of research software.
abstract:
Due to the urgency of the climate crisis, there is a pressing need to reduce the environmental impact of research.  To achieve significant reductions, culture change is required across the entire research landscape, including across the research software community.  Research software contributes to the environmental impact of research, but can research software engineers play a key role in helping to adapt to minimise  this environmental impact?  Would placing RSEs at the core of net-zero roadmaps for digital research infrastructures help the transition?

In this session we will outline the scale of the problem and introduce a number of projects that are aiming to address it (including tools, certification, best practices).  We will introduce a few different ways to get involved including a new Special Interest Group on “Green RSEs” (affiliated with SocRSE) and a wider ESCS community for Environmentally Sustainable Computational Science. 

During the session, we will work together to draft a “green research software roadmap” which sets out our commitment to addressing the topic and helps to identify what the community feels is required to make the urgent progress required.  Development of this roadmap will help us to identify the key priority areas and start to develop plans to address them.  

By bringing a diverse range of voices and opinions together to discuss the next steps in open discussion, we aim to produce an informed roadmap and start to build a community of practice around this vital topic.

title: Deciding on the ideal software environment -- Personal experiences with Anaconda, Docker, virtual machines, and servers
abstract:
The starting point of most computational research projects is deciding what type of system should the software run on. Whether you plan on developing the software in-house or contracting an outside vendor, this is an important decision as it can have an effect on not just the software's development, but the entire lifetime of the project, long after development has completed.
Currently, many options are available to RSEs. Here, we intend to cover:
Anaconda environments
Docker containers
Virtual machines, including Amazon Web Services
Servers
Each of these methods offer different promises of long term maintenance and reproducibility. While the developer's prior experiences will be one important deciding factor, as projects are passed from the initial developer to long-term maintainer(s), other factors become evident.
In this talk, we will give a summary of the options available and share some past personal experiences -- both positive and negative -- with each of them.

title: Good cookies are made with good cookie cutters: Use research software templates to kick-start your research software.
abstract:
There are many guidelines of good practices for developing research software. Most of them are based in similar principles: version control, licences, testing, citation, documentation, etc. But often what you really need is to know how they are implemented in your favourite programming language. Even better: someone creates the basic structure for you, and you can focus on filling in the details.
This is where using Templates can help you getting started with your research software. For example, adding your preferred licence, creating a citation file, and setting up test infrastructure, etc. You still need to add your details to the citation file, write tests, etc. but templates provide you a good starting point.
For example, the Netherlands eScience Center has a Python Template, which sets up the basic structure of a Python package. We are currently working on a similar template  for Julia.
In this talk we want to share our templates  and invite others to use and contribute to them. We'll also collect ideas on how to continue growing these templates  in terms of 
•    Adoption: who uses and maintains them 
•    Scope: how they are used
•    Content: which good practices are currently implemented and what else we can add
Additionally, we want to learn about other similar templates that are used in the RSE community. Do you use software templates to build your research software? Would you like to improve how software templates are used? Join this session and help us build a better research software template ecosystem!

title: Navigating the Legal Landscape: From Research to Commercial Software
abstract:
Disclaimer: This talk does not provide legal advice. It aims to highlight common legal challenges and considerations in software development.
 
In this session, we aim to demystify the essential legal frameworks influencing both research and commercial applications of software, with a particular focus on continuous compliance with data protection laws such as the General Data Protection Regulation (UK GDPR), Data Protection Act (DPA), and Privacy and Electronic Communications Regulations (PECR). We'll delve into the management of Personal Identifying Information (PII) across the software lifecycle and scrutinize intellectual property (IP) rights, including a critical evaluation of the licences of dependencies which often get overlooked yet are pivotal for legal and operational consistency. The presentation will specifically address choosing the right software licences, highlighting differences between MIT, GPL, and AGPL—the latter being crucial for software deployed as a service (SaaS). Participants will receive practical insights based on real-world experiences from two projects that transitioned from development to commercialization, helping them understand the legal landscapes they must navigate, not as legal advice but as practical guidance for avoiding common pitfalls including those related to dependency licences.

title: Level Up Your APIs: Ditch REST, Embrace GraphQL
abstract:
REST has dominated web API design for a long time. However, as applications grow in complexity, REST's limitations make maintaining API and client code difficult. This talk explores why GraphQL is a better choice for building modern web APIs, and how to get up and running with a new GraphQL API service quickly.

GraphQL puts more power in the hands of client developers:

Improved Developer Experience: A single endpoint and a strongly typed schema means that type safety is built in during client development.

Flexibility: Clients can request any combination of data in a single query

Power: Libraries like Relay allow each component to declare its data needs, and the Relay compiler can automatically merge multiple query fragments into a single API request

To support science data sharing and collaboration, the CZI Science engineering team has developed a pair of GraphQL-based tools that make it easy for Science teams to manage their data in the cloud, run processing workflows on their data, and produce strongly typed output:

Platformics:

Express your data schema as a human-readable YAML document using LinkML

Expose your schema via a GraphQL API built on top of the latest-generation Async Python libraries

Metadata is persisted in PostgreSQL and data is stored in S3

Generated code can be customized

title: Open science cloud infrastructure and training for communities in Latin America and Africa
abstract:
The Catalyst Project aims to enable cloud-native research in the biosciences for communities based in Latin America and Africa that are historically marginalised from large-scale scientific infrastructure. Cloud infrastructure can be inaccessible for many reasons, such as the expertise needed to adminster the system, the skills needed to enable cloud-native workflows, and the development of communities of practice centred around contextualised support and knowledge transfer.

This talk shares experiences and lessons learned in delivering a collaborative interactive computing service model, with a particular focus on

- collaborative lesson development
- workshop delivery
- localisation of training material for Latin American communities.

Collaborative lesson development is an approach to lesson design developed by The Carpentries that embeds good practices in curriculum design, open-source collaboration and iterative improvement. We showcase the "Hub Champion Training" lesson based on this framework, intended for community leaders to learn the fundamentals of using and managing their hub, as well as providing user support to their communities.

Workshop delivery for global communities across many time zones can be logistically challenging. We share a few useful tips on lessons learned around the topic of accessibility and engagement.

Localisation of training materials is driven by our partnership with MetaDocencia. Spanish-language content is available to widen access and participation in the training, delivered in the community's preferred language. This talk shares some reflective points on integrating translations into a continuous development workflow.

title: Optimizing Diagnostic Analysis Chain and Data Storage System in the ST40 fusion device
abstract:
Magnetic confinement devices are a promising path to achieve controlled fusion, where plasma, the fourth state of matter, is contained by magnetic fields and heated to extreme temperatures. A comprehensive set of diagnostic systems is essential to generate and control the plasma and sustain fusion reactions. The analyses of the data produced must be deployed in a specific order, considering potential interdependencies and the availability of raw data. The ST40 tokamak, operated by Tokamak Energy Ltd in Oxfordshire, United Kingdom, achieved a milestone by reaching 100 million Kelvin ion temperature[1] , marking a significant breakthrough for spherical tokamaks and highlighting the role of the private sector in fusion energy research. 
In this poster, the Post Pulse Analysis Chain (PPAC) responsible for inter-pulse diagnostic data analysis of ST40 is discussed. PPAC executes over 20 analysis scripts written in Python, MATLAB, Fortran, and IDL and is managed by SLURM workload manager[2] to deal with inter-dependencies and resource allocation. The experimental data is stored in a centralized database called MDSplus[3], accessible to anyone within Tokamak Energy’s network. The poster also gives an overview of various diagnostic analyses and explains the workflow organization, discussing data storage and retrieval strategies in the MDSplus system, and code deployment, showcasing the effectiveness of PPAC for informed experimental operation.

title: Project Management in Research Software - People and Processes
abstract:
Research software projects are incredibly varied - in the number and skill level of people working on them, the time and budget constraints, and the nature of collaboration with the researchers. Each project has different communication needs, schedules and challenges. 

In order to manage a project effectively the project lead has to take all these things into consideration when deciding what tools and processes to put in place to help the project run smoothly, but very few RSEs have training in formal project management, and even fewer in multiple management paradigms.
In this session we hope to gather people who have experience managing or want to learn to manage RSE projects to share their experiences and foster a network of knowledge-sharing to improve project management for everyone.

title: An Introduction to Test-Driven Development
abstract: This workshop will provide an introduction to test-driven development (TDD), a practice that involves writing test code before production code, as a way to guide development and inform the design of software. TDD has grown in popularity in industry over the last couple of decades, with proponents arguing that it leads to robust software that is easier and safer to change. The aim of this workshop is to give people who are curious about TDD, or those who have perhaps dabbled with it a bit, a chance to practice it in a guided setting. Along the way we will highlight what we consider to be some of the benefits it offers, informed by personal experience of employing it on projects. The workshop will be delivered through a combination of short talks, a question-and-answer session, live-coding and an exercise for participants, using Python and the Pytest testing framework.

title: The Machine Learning Packaging Paradigm: Optimising Climate Model Parameterisation Packaging
abstract:
Climate models are essential tools for understanding and predicting the complex Earth system. Parameterisation is required to accurately simulate phenomena such as cloud formation, convection, and radiative transfer that occur on the sub-grid scale. Machine learning (ML) techniques present new opportunities to extract patterns directly from observational data or high-resolution simulations. However, they also present several challenges to ensuring accessible, reusable, reproducible and interoperable software and science. These include design and packaging of ML models, sharing of trained weights, and interoperability between ML frameworks and numerical models.

This poster showcases methods of tackling these challenges following the FAIR principles of software engineering. We present approaches to designing reusable machine learning pipelines with methods capable of accommodating distinct sets of input variables predicting the same target variables using adaptive data loading. Our work also addresses data heterogeneity by developing strategies to handle input variables differing in dimensionality.
We will discuss our pyTorch-Fortran coupling library FTorch facilitating interoperability between python ML and larger Fortran-based models. Another important feature of our work is saving and sharing the trained model weights using Hugging Face for efficient model distribution. We prioritise model reusability through a modular, extensible code design. Reproducibility is ensured via version control, and fixing random seeds. 

Our work showcases interdisciplinary collaboration between climate scientists, ML experts, and software engineers coupling ML parameterizations to the Community Earth System Model (CESM). Tackling these challenges helps improve the accuracy and predictive capabilities of climate models to inform climate change mitigation and adaptation strategies.

title: Enhancing Real-Time Geospatial Big Data Processing and Presentation Through Cloud-Optimised Storage and Formats
abstract:
This talk will explore a transformative approach to handling extensive geospatial data through a streamlined and scalable system architecture. Our method hinges on four foundational elements: cloud-optimised data, object stores, dynamic tile servers, and static web interfaces. We discuss transitioning from traditional scientist-favoured formats like NetCDF and GeoTIFF to advanced, cloud-optimised formats such as Cloud Optimised GeoTIFF and Zarr. These formats are compatible with popular data processing libraries like xarray and rasterio, facilitating parallel processing and efficient access without requiring complete downloads. 
Data storage is achieved using S3-compatible object stores, exemplified by systems like JASMIN (The UK's data analysis facility for environmental science). These stores facilitate the management of substantial datasets by utilising parallelized file systems capable of multiple concurrent reads and supporting HTTP range requests for partial data fetching. This capability is critical for integrating with cloud-optimised files efficiently. 
Additionally, we introduce a novel approach for on-the-fly data tiles generation for frontend applications, utilizing libraries such as rioxarray and rasterio. This enables the deployment of lightweight tile server applications on serverless architectures, dramatically reducing the system's operational footprint. 
This talk will also highlight real-world applications and projects that currently utilize this architecture, demonstrating its effectiveness in processing and presenting multi-gigabyte data files through static web applications. This comprehensive system not only simplifies data handling, but also improves scalability and accessibility, making it a model for future data-intensive applications.

title: RO-Crate: package your research outputs with their metadata
abstract:
RO-Crate is a mechanism for packaging of research outputs along with structured metadata, providing machine-readability and reproducibility following the FAIR principles. RO-Crate is developed through an open community-driven process and reuse existing standards, with a focus on developers and “just enough” Linked Data.

Researchers can distribute their work as an RO-Crate to ensure their data travels with its metadata, so that key components are correctly tracked, archived, and attributed. Data stewards and infrastructure providers can integrate RO-Crate into the projects and platforms they support, to make it easier for researchers to create and consume RO-Crates without knowing the technical background.

The base RO-Crate format is designed to support any domain and any data. Community-developed extensions called “profiles” also allow the creation of more specialised RO-Crates, describing for example workflows, data provenance, or domain-specific data formats.

This poster will outline the RO-Crate project, its basic workings, and some of its most prominent use cases. The aim is to make RSEs at all levels aware of the RO-Crate project, and to start conversations about how it can be integrated into data platforms developed by members of this community.

title: Transforming digital legacy estates to create a more sustainable future
abstract:
The proliferation of digital projects contributes to ever-growing legacy estates for RSE Labs and the management of these estates can present an ongoing challenge. 
In this presentation two RSE teams will discuss how such legacy estates were formed in the King’s College London and University College London contexts, what defines them in terms of size, number and type of projects, the different stakeholders involved, and the resources available to manage them. We will share the wide range of challenges that we encountered, including the time required to undertake such work, lost connections with project leads and the sometimes-difficult conversations needed to make progress. We will discuss other considerations, such as reputational and impact risks, preservation, ethical concerns in terms of what may be best for the project and its users, investigators and other contributors, as well as environmental considerations. 
We will discuss our past and current approaches to addressing these challenges and considerations within each context and the impact these approaches can have on project life cycles and technical strategies. 
We will also address how our experiences inform new project design and funding applications, building long-term planning in from the start. 
Finally, we have a call to action – why you need to begin addressing your legacy estate right now! – and consider long-term sustainability when planning new projects. We will detail the reasons why RSE practitioners, Infrastructure Management roles and RSE Lab management staff should undertake this work - don’t leave it to languish and allow the challenges to grow.

title: rOpenSci Statistical Software Peer Review: The importance and challenge of community engagement.
abstract: Research software is commonly developed by an internal "core" set of people, and often funded by grants with defined end dates.  Research software which survives often does so through being adopted and maintained by broader communities beyond that initial core.  Community engagement is thus vital to the success of research software.  rOpenSci is an organization dedicated to "*Transforming science through open data, software & reproducibility*," and does so through actively nurturing a large and diverse community of research software authors and users.  One of our primary activities is peer review for software in the R computer language, which has been running for almost 10 years.  A recent large, multi-year project expanded the scope of peer review to include statistical software, the primary focus of the R language itself.  This project was led and coordinated by our own core set of rOpenSci people, resulting in a comprehensive system for documenting and assessing statistical software.  As with research software, we will best ensure the long-term survival and relevance of our system through fostering a transition towards community-led maintenance.  This talk will describe challenges and successes in our efforts to engage and expand our community to support our statistical software system, and will draw important parallels with the abiding importance of community engagement in research software development.

title: Agile Methods for RSEs: A formula for scrum-driven software development in research?
abstract:
The University of Manchester RSE department currently services around 70 research projects with the collective pipeline of projects just short of 100. Our department of 48 engineers is built to support research and academics; however, the scale of the operation brings with it complex managerial challenges around managing workloads, maintaining relationships with researchers and ensuring successful, collaborative project delivery. We need to ensure that our RSE developers and senior RSEs (in their capacity as project managers) are prepared and supported with adequate tooling and processes to deliver these projects both flexibly and consistently.  
Consequently, we have implemented our own flavour of “Scrum” within GitHub projects. Scrum is a popular implementation of the principles of agile project management and software development. According to the Scrum Guide (https://www.scrum.org/resources/scrum-guide), Scrum is a lightweight agile framework that helps people, teams and organisations generate value through adaptive solutions for complex problems. This, to us, sounds an awful lot like research!  
In this presentation, we will explain how agile working methods encourage a mindset where changes in requirements are the norm and where the solution development process embraces that change. In Scrum, this is achieved by continuously updating the requirements, working in “timeboxes”, and continuously engaging our academic customers. We have rolled our adaptation out across the department via a practical 2-day course for all RSEs and successfully tested it on an increasing number of research projects.

title: Monitoring and tracking machine learning models for fire sprinkler design in real-time using Simvue
abstract: Machine learning, governed by an optimisation objective, has evolved to handle complex modelling tasks. Managing and monitoring these optimisation processes is challenging, especially when dealing with large-scale simulations or data processing tasks, across domains and compute resources. To address this challenge, the UKAEA has developed Simvue - a generic and configurable real-time tracking and monitoring framework for any simulation or data processing tasks, which can be leveraged to monitor, and control machine learning based optimisation frameworks, providing a unified platform for managing the entire ML workflow. The platform is applicable to both current and legacy applications and is also language- and hardware-agnostic, capable of scaling on to any cloud based or bare-metal architecture. In this poster, we demonstrate how Simvue can be applied to track and monitor an optimisation procedure for fire sprinkler system design, which involves iterative exploration of the simulation design space, parameterised by different sprinkler head designs, droplet size distributions, and water surfactants. Simvue enables researchers to define the optimisation workflow, set up the necessary simulations, and monitor the progress of the optimisation process in real-time across different compute resources. By leveraging Simvue to manage the ML-based optimisation framework, users can streamline the process of identifying optimal fire sprinkler designs, potentially leading to substantial cost savings. The integration of Simvue with ML-based optimisation techniques demonstrates the versatility and effectiveness of the framework in managing complex data processing tasks across various domains with multi-fidelity resources.

title: Harnessing Data Visualization for Public Engagement a Case Study: Air Quality Stripes
abstract:
Data visualisation can serve as a powerful conduit for communicating complex information to diverse audiences.  Research software engineers are often well placed to help researchers visualise complex datasets in a clear and impactful way.  Such visualisations not only enhance accessibility but also foster public engagement and awareness.
In this work we show an example of such a collaboration.  Inspired by the well known Climate Warming Stripes images which vividly show the global temperature change (https://www.reading.ac.uk/planet/climate-resources/climate-stripes) since 1850, we present the Air Quality Stripes, a series of visualisations which depict historical changes in air pollution concentrations from 1850-2021.  These illustrations, produced from publicly available data (UKESM1 CMIP6 ensemble dataset), clearly show the changing trends in air pollution in different cities.  Overall air pollution in Europe and North America was worst in the 1940-1960s but has responded to increased legislation.  Unfortunately air pollution concentrations in many parts of Africa and Asia are rising at a concerning level. These images are being used to stimulate discussions around air quality and inequality around the globe.  Images were produced using Jupyter notebooks on the JASMIN data service.  Input from an experienced RSE was core to the data manipulation, processing and visualisation required to realise this idea. 
These visualizations serve as catalysts for discussions surrounding air quality and societal inequalities worldwide. This presentation underscores the immense potential for RSEs to actively contribute to translating research into engaging and accessible material, thereby fostering broader awareness and understanding of critical global issues.

title: Creating greener software
abstract:
Green computing is a very broad term encompassing endeavours such as the development and use of energy efficient hardware, the powering of computing infrastructure with renewable energy sources, the repurposing and recycling of computing assets, to extracting benefit from the excess heat produced by HPC systems for example.
On the software side there are decisions a software engineer can make to create software that is more environmentally friendly. These decisions relate to various aspects of the software engineering process such as design and coding choices, choice of programming language, as well as monitoring and testing. 
Highlighted here are some practical and general considerations to employ during the development cycle that can help lead to more energy efficient software. For illustrative purposes a comparison of the energy efficiency of some coding test cases is also presented.
